utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If there are no preliminaries, the witness can be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber has not yet decided on the admission of some of the Philipps -- the report and the charts and the explanatory notes. Are there objections? Let me take it one by one P451, that is the two charts which are in one document, one for 1992, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would have the same objections we have in our written submissions, Your Honour, from before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would that be true for the explanatory notes P452 and P453 as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then also for the alphabetical lists, the P454 and P455?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The Chamber will decide on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sivac. Mr. Sivac, before we continue, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Shin, if you're ready, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to a particular topic I'll ask you some questions about. Was there a time when about 12 buses of persons arrived at Omarska camp while you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime after the 20th of July we were in a room with Mujo Murha and there was a sound coming from nearby, the sound of bus engines. Shortly afterwards, we heard guards shouting, we heard noise. The guards were taking out of the buses that had arrived at Omarska and only later would we learn that the buses were packed with the inhabitants of the village of Brdo on the left bank of the Sana River, who had been picked up in those villages when the ethnic cleansing began there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you explain how it is that you learned that these persons were from Brdo?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later at the Omarska camp I came across a number of my acquaintances from Brdo who arrived in those buses to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of those persons whom you recognised in Omarska camp from Brdo?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I talked to them. That was Vahid Rizvanovic, a colleague of mine who worked for the security service; Mehmed Crljenkovic, aka Mesa, and there were a few other people from Brdo who had survived the arrival to the camp Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What happened to those persons from Brdo who arrived in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken out in groups and lined up against a wall precisely in the room where we were. Then we heard guards shouting, they cocked their weapons, we heard horrible thumps of something being thrown against the wall, we heard cries, screams, cries for help, and something that made it very clear to us was that on arrival to the Omarska camp they had to pass through this reception procedure, which means, in other words, that they had to be beaten up properly, unfortunately. Some of those people did not survive that, that beating up. They succumbed immediately on the spot next to the wall. Later on, we called this wall the wailing and screaming wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, in the translation your answer has it that these persons were taken out in groups and lined against a wall -- there's a word unclear. Lined up against a wall in the room where we were. Were these persons lined up in the room that you were or were they somewhere else? And if somewhere else, could you explain exactly where they were?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was in the room with Burho and Mujo and that wall was the outer wall of the room where we were. It was located on the north side and the wall was very thin. At the upper level of this room were small windows through which we received air because it was horribly hot inside and there was a huge crowd of people. Before that, the guards allowed us to open those windows in order to have as much air as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You explained that some of these persons succumbed immediately on the spot next to the wall. Did you see any bodies at any point from these persons?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, the following day, when we were going from the tarmac to answer the call of nature, the guards took us past the white house to do it there. And then next to the white house we saw a rather large group of dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, I would now like to move to another topic relating to certain names of persons who may have been in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: May I ask the Court Officer, please, to place 65 ter 28532 on the screen. If possible for the witness could we focus on the B/C/S translation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, are you able to read that page on your screen? If you could just indicate yes or no and I'll ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you recall that I asked you about a list of certain names during preparation for your testimony here? If you could just indicate yes or no whether you recall that, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you please take a moment to review the information next to the names and then indicate where the information, although brief, is accurate?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the information is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would tender this -- tender into evidence 65 ter 28532.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28532 becomes Exhibit P488, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: May I ask the Court Officer to place 65 ter 28533 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, could you please take a moment to review this list of names and -- let me ask you first: Do you recall that we discussed these names during the preparation for your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could you please take a moment to review the information next to these names and then indicate whether the information - again, although it is brief - whether that information is accurate.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only the first name on the list reads Ljubija Solaja. I think that Miroslav -- oh, now I see that it has been corrected. He was originally from Ljubija and his name is written here as Ljubija Solaja, but underneath that we see his correct name which is Miroslav Solaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, would you like any more time to review the brief information placed next to the names or are you able to say that it is otherwise accurate?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, completely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would also tender into evidence 65 ter 28533.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no objections, but I have one question. If we read a name and the comment is "probably typo for Pehadzic," then we see that "Alija Behadzic" should be "Pehadzic," but what then? I mean, what's then the probative value? Is that a -- was that person in Omarska? Was that person killed? Was that person wounded? Was that a guard at Omarska? What we -- I do not understand that part of your list. For the others I do understand, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The name Alija Pehadzic is referred to elsewhere and I will be in a position to provide that information as necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that is then a correction to the name Behadzic found elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there are no objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28533 becomes Exhibit P489 [Realtime transcript read in error "P589"], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that brings me to a total of half an hour and that completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shin. Mr. Lukic, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour. Just give me half a minute to organise myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sivac, you'll be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May we begin?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we may.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We haven't seen each other for ten years.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Time flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now I'm going to go back to the list, or rather, the two lists shown to you by the OTP this morning, and these are the lists of people whom you identified as being in Omarska. The document numbers are 28532 and 28533, just to remind you. Now, is it true that you did not see the killing of those people, you only heard of that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to wait a little after your question for the interpretation to finish and then I'll start. No, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for those who read the transcript later, it is P588 and P589, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour 4, if I may just -- it's P488 and P489.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it appears wrongly on the transcript. 488 is on page 5, line 6; and then on page 6, line 18, it says "P489" but that apparently is a -- "589" that apparently is a mistake. 65 ter 28533 has been assigned P489 and is admitted under that number. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic. The executioners did not allow anyone to watch while they were killing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor's office tendered your statement and portions of the transcript; however, some portions that we would like to ask you about are not included therein. So let us go through that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly seek assistance with regard -- with 65 ter number of the witness statement which is 28478, but unfortunately I haven't written down the P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, now I have it. It's P480.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I think that takes care of my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Earlier you said that Hasan Talundzic was the first Muslim appointed to the post of the SUP chief in Prijedor. Do you remember that testimony of yours?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall who Sead Besic was?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that he was at the head of the Prijedor SUP before Mr. Talundzic and that he was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic. He only had a Muslim name but he declared himself a Yugoslav. According to the 1974 constitution, he was entitled to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The fact is that he was at the head of the Prijedor SUP after Rajko Zigic left that post; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Rajko Zizic passed away he led the SUP for a brief period of time, and then after the first democratic election that post was filled by the party SDA, the Party of Democratic Action, and they appointed Hasan Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that Mr. Sead Besic was promoted and referred to the position of the CSB Banja Luka chief?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was promoted to a higher rank, but I do know that he was transferred to work at the State Security Service in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the League of Communists while you were working at the SUP just like everybody else; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After multi-party elections, were you a member of any other party?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now something relating to the geography of Prijedor. Stari Grad, the old town, was between 800 and 1.000 metres away from the place of your residence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my initial impression, but I think the distance is shorter. Now when I go to visit these places, I often realise that it's much shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How shorter approximately, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 300 and 500 metres. There is the beginning of the Stari Grad neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the day of attack on Prijedor the 30th of May you were in Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that was not an attack on Prijedor. That was an attempt to liberate Prijedor and to install into power the legally elected representatives of those authorities. On that morning I was in my flat and I stayed there the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were first arrested on the 12th of May, 1992, by members of the Prijedor SUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They took you to the SUP building, handed over to Ranko Mijic, the chief of the criminal investigation police?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the chief of the criminal investigation service, Ranko Mijic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were released from Omarska you talked with Milos Jankovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when I was first released or do you mean after my final release?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you talk with Milos Jankovic on the 10th of June, which means that would be after your first release?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember if it was after the first release, but I don't think it was. I think that I spoke with Milos Jankovic much, much later, in September or October 1992, just before I left Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then that would have to be corrected. That means after your second release?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that you asked him who signed your arrest warrant?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I asked him that, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that he told you that anyone from the SUP could have signed that warrant?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less that was his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you said that most often the orders were signed by the Crisis Staff and people like Simo Drljaca, Dule Jankovic, and Rajko Mijic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was what Milos Jankovic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca, Dure Jankovic, and Ranko Mijic were all members of the Prijedor SUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you try to always guide the Judges to the relevant pages of P480 so that we are able -- for example, if you say "should this be corrected," so that we know exactly what is there to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness just corrected me that it was after his second release, not after his first release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and -- but you are talking about the statement. Since you did not guide us to where it is in the statement, we do not know what is reflected in the statement immediately and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can see 1D408 on our screens and Your Honours would see that line of questions I just went through.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or we can see P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We work --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At page 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well I have it on my screen but -- that's no problem, but I would like to know which page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's page 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the original page number, do you have that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The original page number is transcript number 6617, lines 5 to 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the redacted portion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly, that's why I have to use 1D408.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From this one we need page 67, lines 5 to 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it's of assistance to my counsel, this refers to an arrest on the 10th of June, so perhaps that may be useful to clarify any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we just did it with the witness. He guided us that this conversation took place after his second release. My question was in relation to the first release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Could we go to the next page in the document which is on the screen, and that is 1D480 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 408.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to have a look at lines 14 through 18. I'll read it out in English so that you can receive proper interpretation. The question was this: [In English] "Was it publicly announced who was the leadership of the municipality at that time? Was that ever discussed on the radio? Or who was giving orders for the events in Prijedor?" And your answer at line 17, I quote: "All these things happened as a result of the directives issued by the Crisis Staff." [Interpretation] My question is whether you accept this part of your testimony in view of the assessment you had made?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what period does this refer to, this question? Or is this merely an assertion of yours? I can expand if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll guide you. As of the moment when the Crisis Staff was established, which was sometime after the 20th or 22nd of April when the Prijedor municipality Crisis Staff was established.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the official date, but the Crisis Staff had existed before. It's just that they worked covertly. They were just waiting for the right moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But while they were working covertly, they were not making public announcements I presume. So we are talking about an announcement which is after the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When such announcements or ultimatums were cunningly signed by the information secretariat attached to the newly established Serb municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you accept this part of your testimony, the part I just read out?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Crisis Staffs issued ultimatums and announcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] "All these things happened as a result of the directives issued by the Crisis Staff." [Interpretation] There was discussion about orders concerning the events in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's crystal clear. I can repeat. All those directives and instructions issued after the take-over were aimed at the inhabitants of Prijedor municipality. First curfew was introduced; second, all media was put under control, that is to say Radio Prijedor and the "Kozarski Vijesnik" newspaper; thirdly, there was a general call-up for the Serbian population; fourthly, all non-Serbs had to hand-over their weapons to the barracks in Urije, those who were supposed to arrive in convoys bringing in weapons were supposed to post white flags; fifthly, before the 20th of May all economic activity was to cease and workers allowed to go home. All schools and kindergartens had to stop working before the 20th of May. Anyone of sound mind in Prijedor could realise what was in store.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We haven't established whether you confirm what you had stated earlier, which was that it all came as part of directives and instructions of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had an informant of mine, a source, and I know that the first time the name "Crisis Staff" appeared officially in documents around the 12th or the 13th of May. All those ultimatums which were basically drafted by the Crisis Staff were issued together with the information secretariat. It was a very cunning procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time immediately before the conflict, but after the war had started in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were frequent skirmishes and a lot of propaganda; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your observation? Did people become distrustful of one another?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation spread throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and the same thing applied to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How about the inter-ethnic relations between the peoples, did they become contaminated?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was specifically obvious in Prijedor because it used to be a very tolerant environment where all ethnic communities lived together; however, contaminated by the propaganda which came from Serbia and Pale as well as from Prijedor itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me put the next question to you. Is it correct that inter-ethnic relations were quite bad as early as 1991?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there no arguments or conflicts concerning mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very complex issue. The problem was an ideological one. All Serbs wanted to live in a Greater Serbia which would basically be some kind of ex-Yugoslavia, whereas all other ethnicities in line with the decisions of the international community and its representatives in Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted to become independent, to see Bosnia and Herzegovina and -- become an independent state like Croatia and Slovenia had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sivac, you are an old time Prijedor resident. Was it your impression at the time that many crimes were committed out of revenge?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the clashes began.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clashes, that's a different thing. Before the clashes and during the time of expectation, if I can put it that way, in 1991 - or time of anticipation, whenever Serb warriors returned from the theatre of war in Slavonia, in Croatia, there were always serious incidents and murders out of revenge, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the war contribute to the fact that criminals found fruitful ground for robbing and looting?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Criminals from Prijedor - and I know them all because I had worked for 20 years for the security service - immediately took part in those Serb army units. They went to wage war in Western Slavonia, not because of their ideological beliefs; they went to loot and to be issued with weapons after the fact they were mobilised. Once they returned from war, they used those weapons to do evil and to loot. One of the most notorious units that was part of the 43rd Brigade and later the 5th Kozara Brigade was the Suha Rebra [phoen] unit. They were criminals from Bosanski Novi who had been mobilised into the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you something about your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P480, please. We need the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In lines 7 through 10 you discuss Milos Jankovic. You say that it was his task to ethnically cleanse your section where you worked. When did Milos Jankovic arrive in your section or, firstly, what was the title of your department? We have "section" here.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the organisational chart it was the communications centre for encryption. I told you earlier that Milos Jankovic was appointed head of that part of service in 1983, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you left in 1989?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st of January, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During what period was Jankovic engaged in ethnically cleansing your organisation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had received any orders to do that. I think it was his personal choice. I and a colleague of mine asked to be transferred. We wanted to leave the service, thus leaving only one Muslim person behind. Serbs were placed in our positions. It used to be a service which was very careful of the ethnic key and its application, whereas during that period of time it basically became a service of only one ethnicity where only one Muslim remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So apparently you and another Muslim left the section?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, his name appears in my previous testimony. If need be, I can repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have the name. Were any Serbs and Croats leaving the service at the same time? Did anyone retire?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from my part of the service. I'm only discussing my section. As for the entire security service, of course everyone made use of their legal right to retire when they believed they had met the conditions to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was Jankovic doing this, that is to say, was he ethnically cleansing the service while Sead Besic was his superior who was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was doing it precisely at the time when Sead Besic was the head of the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I presume that Milos Jankovic too was a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is likely. He wouldn't have been employed in our service had he not been a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This conduct of his, was it not unacceptable according to the ideology of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, after 1991 and Tito's death, the League of Communists of Yugoslavia was disintegrating, it was falling apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The fact is that it was one-party until the multi-party elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not in the same format and not in the same way that they did while Tito was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Milos Jankovic continue this practice even when Hasan Talundzic was appointed his chief?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did, but please do not ask me about that period because I had already left the security service by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 11 of the compilation of transcript which constitutes your statement, lines 24 and 25, you speak about the columns of people coming from Raskovac and Skela. They were all arriving to Prijedor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those people were from Prijedor. These are just neighbourhoods in Prijedor, in the suburbs of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So where were they coming then to?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were coming from these suburban areas, in the area before the building where I lived which is the very centre of Prijedor town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any fightings in their neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no fighting either in Raskovac, Skela, or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last name of the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness please repeat the last name he mentioned of that neighbourhood. You said Raskovac, Skela, or ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Zagrad, not Stari Grad. Stari Grad is a different area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned the curfew. Is it true that the curfew was applicable to all civilians and that Serb, Croat, or Muslim civilians were not allowed to move around after the curfew?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was supposed to be, but all that was applicable to non-Serbs only. All the Serbs were wearing uniforms and nobody could have prohibited them from moving after the curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I presume that there were Serbs with work obligation, women who were not dressed in uniforms, were they the subject of that same curfew? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few of them. There were only very few of them who had work obligation. For the most part the Serb population was in uniform already and had weapons issued to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 69 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you received only answer to half of your question. Were the Serbian women allowed to move around, Mr. Sivac? If you look at Mr. Lukic, but I'm putting the question which -- of course it's in translation to you, but -- yes. Were the Serbian women free to move around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know, Your Honour. During the curfew I stayed indoors in my flat, and I had no way of seeing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 69, please, of your statement, 6690. We need lines 21 through 25. You spoke about Serbs who were returning from the front line, mostly tank crews who came to Trnopolje to pick women and young girls. During the period that you are talking about you were not in Trnopolje - is that correct? - you just heard this second hand.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived at Trnopolje we received this information from the inmates who had been in Trnopolje at that specific time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we need next page, which is page 70, lines 3 and 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- where you say that if anyone were to leave Trnopolje had to fulfil a number of conditions. One of the conditions was to hand over his money and other valuables. In your view, was that a criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know a number of people who managed to leave the Trnopolje camp in that manner. Yes, it was a criminal activity that was pursued by Slobodan Kuruzovic and the Balaban brothers in the Trnopolje camp who were military policemen and who were his escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself hand over the money in order to be released or did you leave the camp in some other way?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the camp in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On this same page, page 70, you spoke about the wired fence that was surrounding one part of the area where people were placed. This wired fence in Trnopolje that you described, was it pulled down before the arrival of TV crews and foreign journalists or was that done after they had left?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't know which TV crew you're referring to because several TV crews and groups of journalists visited Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here you mention that Zeljko Mejakic, the Omarska commander had brought several foreign TV crews.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation. Mr. Lukic, Zeljko Mejakic did indeed bring a number of journalists but only a few days later when this wire fence was removed. I understood that you asked me about the visit by Penny Marshal and that was the time when this wire fence was still in existence. After spending a few days at Trnopolje camp, the administration of the camp decided in the aftermath of the broadcast of the shots there made by Penny Marshal, I suppose that that was the time when the administration decided to remove the fence. So a few days after that, this crew led by the camp commander, Zeljko Mejakic, arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if this would be a suitable time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The break will be slightly longer today for very practical reasons. Could the witness already follow the usher. We take a break of approximately a half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time for the following, and I'm addressing mainly the Defence. But for a number of MFI's, the parties have not yet provided English translations or final English translations. The parties are instructed to review the list of the following MFI's and report back to the Chamber by next Tuesday. It's about D65, D67, D59, D47, D48, D40, and D81.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, once you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I am ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, now I'd like to discuss Kozarac with you because that's also a subject that you addressed in your statement. Do you know that in Kozarac there were 3.500 registered combatants as part of the Muslim Bosniak forces of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information is wrong. That's a fabrication that the media disseminated, and I'm referring here to Simo Drljaca and the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to how many combatants there were?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have accurate information, but I'm sure that the number was far, far lower than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it a fact that on the 25th of May the military column moving towards Prijedor was attacked and the column was coming from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information is incorrect too. This was taken only as a pretext and as an excuse to shell and attack Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So was the army from Banja Luka or were they from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this, Mr. Lukic: The entire main road between Prijedor and Banja Luka at the time was controlled by the VRS and it was completely passable and accessible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was if you knew whether those military personnel were from Banja Luka or from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you that there was no army and there was no convoy. That's a fabrication that was disseminated in order to raise tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true -- is it true that the first conflict broke out in Jakupovici?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. Only towards the end of the ethnic cleansing of Kozarac a conflict broke out in Jakupovici. That was a revenge of Momcilo Radinovic, aka Cica, and a group of the residents of Jakupovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Had you heard that soldier Jovan Zgonjanin was killed and he was at the head of the column in a truck?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information is also wrong, Mr. Lukic. Even the most zealous purveyors and conveyers of this information, such as "Kozarski Vjesnik" and Radio Prijedor said that only something allegedly happened in general terms, that a column had allegedly been attacked. And the name of the soldier that you mention is completely wrong because if that were true they would have published his name. This soldier was killed during the ethnic cleansing of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were not in Kozarac at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. The capture of Kozarac took place and I was following the events through the media only. There was almost a live broadcast provided by Radio Prijedor of the Serb capture of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you also did not take part in the arming of people of Kozarac and that you don't know what kind of weapons they had?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not take part in the army -- arming of any group. According to the information that I have, the people of Kozarac who had a number of weapons, those weapons were mostly infantry weapons and a few Zoljas, rocket-launchers, that each of the member had in his arsenal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that at one point on the 25th of May the fighting stopped and that people who put up resistance in Kozarac were called upon to surrender and end the fighting?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the request of Osmo Didovic, the police commander of Kozarac who used radio communication to get in touch with Radmilo Zeljaja who was leading the operation of the capture of Kozarac, the fighting was suspended for a while; however, Zeljaja put forth a condition that the policemen from the Kozarac police station must surrender unconditionally at the -- with -- led by Mr. Didovic. At the time it was under the police station of Prijedor, and during peace time it was manned only by ten policemen. The commander of the Kozarac police station, Osmo Didovic, led the column of the Kozarac police officers. And at the forward command post where Radmilo Zeljaja was he -- they surrendered themselves directly to him. However, that was not enough and they were executed in the vicinity of that command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you were told by others; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, the negotiations failed and the fighting resumed on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Osmo Didovic and the group of policemen surrendered and when the rest heard what had happened to them, there was panic. Any kind of resistance in Kozarac had been dealt with much before that and the population was simply now trying to save their lives because the shelling was resumed. There was random shelling of the entire area of Kozarac. Some fled in panic towards Mount Kozara while others surrendered to the Serb army and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that many civilians arrived in Prijedor after the fighting was stopped?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite interesting. Only a small portion of the population managed to reach Prijedor by routes unknown to me. However, a small group was placed in the area of Puharska while another bigger group which was in front of the gym in Prijedor was put on buses and taken to the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that those wounded in Kozarac were taken to the hospital in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have firsthand information on that account. The drivers who drove the two ambulances told me about that in the camp. Near the forward command post where Radmilo Zeljaja was, as well as the command of Serb attacks on Kozarac, they were made to abandon their ambulances and taken to the camp. Those wounded who were in the ambulances were killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it is your testimony today that the wounded from Kozarac were not taken to the Prijedor hospital?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know about the two vehicles, and if you want me to I can cite the names of the drivers. The two vehicles were destroyed and the wounded people inside killed. I don't know whether some other people managed to reach the Prijedor hospital by other means or in another way - that may well be - but I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a counter attack on Kozarac in an attempt to get it back by Muslim forces headed by Kemal Alagic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this is a farce, it's ridiculous. Kemal Alagic -- well, Divjak was in the area of Ljubija. In order to reach Kozarac -- well, it was impossible. It's not true. It was a fabrication which may have been carried by the media. I've never heard of that and it never came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you hear that on the 3rd of May an SDA war staff was formed in Hambarine and their seat was in a bunker on Orahovo hill?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear this for the first time and I was not a member of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the commander of units in Kozarac was Sead Cirkin who at the time was an active-duty military officer?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard. Once he left the JNA he went back to his native town of Kozarac in an attempt to establish some kind of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The policeman from Kozarac whom you mentioned took part in the fighting; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. It was their duty to protect the civilians and the population of Kozarac village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of them were killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be. I don't know about that, but I do know about the group headed by their commander. I know that they were cruelly murdered after they had surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 94 we have a redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D414, page 80. It is transcript page 13258 of the 16th of August, 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There you say -- you begin discussing Hambarine. [In English] "There was still a decree in force at the time issued by the legal authorities at the municipal level in Prijedor, stating that in the enclave where the Muslims were in the majority, there had to be check-points formed which were to serve to check any Serb soldiers who frequently tried to enter the enclave drunk and to prevent them from doing so. They were supposed to hand over their weapons at such check-points and on their way out they would be given their weapons back." [Interpretation] Please tell us where we can find this decree or whatever the legal document was called.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That decree or that regulation or that approval for check-points to be established in ethnically pure enclaves was put into force by the illegally elected authorities with the participation of Serbs because there were frequent complaints by the residents, inhabitants of those enclaves, of such incidents taking place. It is not only that Muslims had a right to set up check-points in such situations, but also Serbs in their ethnically pure Serb enclaves were entitled to establish such check-points to control entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see that decree?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. However, such information was broadcast on Radio Prijedor. It was also published in the "Kozarski Vjesnik" newspaper in January or February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know that SFOR had collected all documentation pertaining to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor as well as the Prijedor SUP and Kozarski Vjesnik as well as that of the hospital in Prijedor. Such a legal document has never been shown here.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of documents they found. I do know, however, that it was agreed by the then-authorities, the legally elected authorities and representatives in Prijedor to have it done. In such arrangements, Radmilo Zeljaja and Vladimir Arsic who were the barracks commanders also took part as well as other commanders of the Serb war-time units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, would you please remind Mr. Mladic that there should be no discussions, no consultations, no talking in court, consultations to be during the break. This is the last warning for today. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the same document, page 81, which is the next page, you discuss an incident at a check-point in Hambarine. You say that there were six drunken Serbs in a single car who caused an incident. The patrolman at the check-point asked them to surrender their weapons, promising that they would return them once they came back. However, the people in the vehicle opened fire and the result was two dead Serb soldiers and a number of wounded. That is lines 1 through 6 on this page. First of all, do you know now that there were two Croats in that vehicle as well?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew it the very day of the incident. I knew that there were two Croats who were members of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many Muslims were wounded in that incident?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I have, there were three wounded Muslims. One was called Ferid Sikiric who was seriously wounded and transported to the Prijedor hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know the names of the other two?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one was a Ejupovic and another Ramulic, Aziz Aliskovic, and another two men, cousins of his, who were also present at the check-point when the incident took place fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our information is to the extent that no Muslims were wounded and the Serbs did not open fire whatsoever. Do you assert that that is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Here in the courtroom I had an opportunity to view some footage where Ferid Sikiric was interviewed in the Prijedor hospital following his wounding. In detail he explained how things developed. For the Court's benefit, Ferid Sikiric, once he had provided an interview for the Serbian television, was taken from the Prijedor hospital and killed somewhere outside the hospital despite the fact that he had been seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber feels that it is not very much assisted by having the two versions where this witness apparently has no firsthand knowledge of much of it. Now, of course, hearsay is not prohibited, but then to hear your version and then the witness saying that it's not true and that he saw once on television this or that. Let's try and stick as close as possible to what the facts are the witness observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time of call-ups in the fall of 1991, in September, the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina were against the JNA; is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not. Muslims in Bosnia were against being mobilised. They were not against the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the leadership of the SDA in Prijedor was against the presence of the JNA in the area of Prijedor municipality in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They simply wanted that the JNA, which was still the Yugoslav People's Army, to conduct themselves in a fair and appropriate manner when found in such a large town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the SDA president in Prijedor tried to stop a JNA column as early as July or August 1991?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of such columns used force on the streets of Prijedor. It was a show of strength. The tanks paced or rolled up and down the streets of Prijedor causing fear and panic. Upset by such military conduct, Mirza Mujadzic used his own vehicle and placed it in the middle of one of the streets. By that fact alone, he managed to stopped the tanks. There was a brief verbal argument and the situation was tense. However, after a short while the tanks went on their way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Due to the tensions and everything that was going on in Bosnia, people of all ethnicities were leaving Bosnia and Prijedor as early as the beginning of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct. The Serbs were not leaving Prijedor. Prijedor was abandoned only by Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The head of the National Defence Secretariat as of the multi-party elections in 1990 was Becir Medunjanin; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He was an SDA member?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the head of military unit was a Serb, Zeljaja or Arsic, either of the two?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they rotated in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Military units could not be manned without the participation of Becir Medunjanin because he had the records of military conscripts in his hands?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the records of able-bodied men were kept at the Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that Medunjanin obstructed as much as he could the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Becir Medunjanin, chief of the draft office in Prijedor, was following the instructions that he was receiving from the republican secretariat in Sarajevo and he had to comply with their decisions. You know the doctrine that was in place in the former state, which is to say that all military structures were under the control of civilian authorities, at least that's how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The instructions that Medunjanin was receiving were such that he was instructed to obstruct the mobilisation, those received from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, neither Zeljaja nor Arsic had a right to organise the mobilisation in their own way. That required a decision to be taken by the Secretariat for National Defence or at least in agreement with them. As it is, it would have been a private army of Zeljaja or Arsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then based on what did they request those lists? Was it somebody's decision or did they decide themselves to carry out a kind of private mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why they asked for those lists because all these war time units that they headed were well manned. They were very actively involved in the theatre of war in Western Slavonia and Croatia in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't put my question correctly. Is it true that the mobilisation carried out in 1991 in September and in early 1992 was legal?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are reading only one section of that law. Your Honours, let me tell you this: It is true that there is an article in the said law which says that if there is an attack on Yugoslavia, a general mobilisation must be carried out and all able-bodied men must respond to it. However, here Mr. Lukic omitted to read further on. There's another article in the law which says that if, or rather, it reads like this: No one has the right to mobilise a person to join a military formation that would go out and commit crimes in contravention of the international conventions and laws on human rights to which Yugoslavia was a signatory. This time around the political leadership in Sarajevo tried to explain it in this manner: By saying that nobody attacked Yugoslavia and therefore no one is bound to respond to the mobilisation, because if one goes to fight in a war you will have to kill members of the peoples who only a few months before that used to live side by side with us. That law could be applied only in the event of an external attack on Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have read quite a few military regulations, but I have never come across such a provision. Can you please enlighten me and tell me which law you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we're entering in a legal debate rather than anything else. I don't know whether this witness who may have opinions about these matters but is not called as an expert in these matters, to what extent this witness can assist us. Just for you to know that this is of some concern to me. I'm not going to stop you because -- but please be aware of the limited importance of a debate with a non-trained lawyer in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would have only one follow-up question. Actually, I would let the witness to answer to quote the law where he said he found this article or provision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If he's able to do so, he's invited to do so. Do you have the article you just quoted -- you referred to, do you have -- can you quote it? Do you have the text somewhere available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That answers the question. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Can we please have in e-court Exhibit 1D411. We need page 3, transcript number 6777.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In line 9 to 13 you say: [In English] "All those who refused to join the Serb army who were Muslims and Croats were accused chiefly of this. This was one of the chief allegations made against them, one of the main reasons for their being taken to the camps, to Omarska and Keraterm." [Interpretation] And then in line 4 you say the following: [In English] "Let me explain why they needed those lists. Later on in 1992 when the Serb Democratic Party with the help of the army and police took over power in Prijedor, they made use of these lists to accuse all those who had not reported -- who had not responded to the call-up ..." [Interpretation] Would you say again today that the main reason for people being detained and imprisoned at Omarska and Keraterm was that they failed to respond to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the only reason. That was only one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that all Muslim journalists, Muslim and Croat journalists, from September 1991 onwards used to refer to the JNA in their reports as the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't know which journalists you have in mind, all the journalists in Bosnia-Herzegovina or just the journalists from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 4 of this document which is the next page. The transcript page is 6778 and we need lines 9 to 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The question was: [In English] "Your television company, from the beginning of September 1991, did it tell you when you were reporting on the JNA, to use the term 'The former JNA'?" And your response in lines 12 and 13 was, I quote: "Yes. Yes. All the journalists of Bosniak and Croatian nationality used this term." So can you please tell us, does this refer to Prijedor or was it something that came from the central office in Sarajevo, meaning that it pertained to the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also is your statement correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the decision by the central office in Sarajevo and that's how the former Yugoslav army was designated, not only by the Muslim journalists but also by the Serbs who stayed behind in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Central office of what? Witness, could you ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the editorial office of Sarajevo television with whom we maintained a permanent contact and that was the news and political section of TV Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was this use of this word, was that limited to this television company or was it also in newspapers and was it more broadly applied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was applied in the print media as well, but I don't know exactly. Believe me, I cannot remember when such recommendation came from the editorial office, whether that was in 1991 or maybe much, much later. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The reason why I'm asking because the question by which Mr. Lukic introduced the matter was by a general reference to journalists, whereas the questions here seem to focus on the television company. So therefore I would -- wanted to understand how broad or narrow this habit was. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] We need page 5 now in this document, 1D414. The transcript page is 6779 and we need lines 13 to 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say: [In English] "... I visited and I had an opportunity to visit only a few polling stations, a large number of Serbs voted for an independent and sovereign Bosnia." [Interpretation] So you said today that the Serbs were in favour of remaining within Yugoslavia. Now here you said that a large number of Serbs voted in favour of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you reconcile these two assertions?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it can be explained very easily. The plebiscite that the Serbs had organised was completely unconstitutional and illegal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we -- when I read your answer at the time is that: " ... I think that according to the statements made by members of the electoral commissions I visited, and I had an opportunity to visit only a few polling stations, a large number of Serbs voted for an independent and sovereign Bosnia." So what apparently the witness is doing is quoting what the members of the electoral commissions stated, whereas in your question, Mr. Lukic, you asked: "Now here you said that a large number of Serbs voted in favour of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." That's not what the witness said. The witness said is that this was what the members of the electoral commission told him, and further in that answer it's clear that he cannot quantify that in any way. Let's remain very precise on questions and let's also try to avoid to move away very much to background and issues which are more in the margin of the testimony of this witness rather than to focus on the core of the testimony of this witness. I must immediately add to that, Mr. Lukic, that the way in which the Prosecution presented this evidence certainly also adds to this confusion so I'm just trying to get things on track as good as I can. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will withdraw the question and I will pose different question that is more in connection with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sivac, what were you told by the members of these commissions, can you recall? How many Serbs were counted at those polling stations and how was it possible to know what their vote was because it was a secret ballot?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the members of the commissions knew all their Serb neighbours who came to vote and on the basis of that they provided this kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for the voters to vote either in favour or against? Do they know exactly how many Serbs turned out?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't know how many people turned out, but they know that Serbs took part in the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I again try to cut this short. What really is the dispute between the parties? Is it the position of the Prosecution that the Serbs by -- in any substantial way participated in this referendum? And is it the position of the Prosecution that the Serbs by a majority were in favour of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina ? Is that the position of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may answer in brief, that was not the focus or the purpose that we had tendered the -- this witness's evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not my question --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- how you focused, but whether that's the position, if that's the case, of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I may consult briefly with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. No, Your Honour, that is not our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Lukic, many of your questions seem to focus on perhaps a few remarks by the witness but seems not to address anything that is in dispute between Prosecution and Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So would you please move on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sivac, let's move on. I wanted to ask you about Donja Puharska which is a Muslim village. Is it correct that as early as March 1992 there were night guards in that village?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Puharska is not a village; it is a neighbourhood of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apologies then. Is it correct that in Puharska, part of Prijedor -- first of all, is it a Muslim part of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are about 70 per cent Muslims and 30 per cent Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in March 1992 there were night guards in that part of Prijedor and night patrols?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because I did not reside in that part of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 6 of this document, please, which is 1D411. It is transcript page 6780.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The question begins in line 9 and concludes in line 10 and then the answer, which is somewhat long, goes on up to line 23 and then continues in 25. The question is: [In English] "Do you know that in March 1992 the villages of Donja Puharska were already holding night patrols?" And the question continues in line 24 and it says: "Is your answer to my question yes?" And line 25 the answer was: "Yes, it is." [Interpretation] Does this refresh your memory? You had previously responded to the same kind of question with a yes.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I can say now is that I accept the answer I provided before because my memory was better at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think we are close to where we need a break. Could you find a suitable moment within the next two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a suitable moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break but not until after the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are we on track as far as timing is concerned? I think your estimate was three hours -- three and a half -- two and a half, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would accept that three-hour estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, how generous of you, Mr. Lukic. Could you give us an indication?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I should finish in another -- in another hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we take a break and we resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, it is not the first time that the Chamber had to wait for a substantial time before we could start. If you next time would again use the toilet facilities at the end of the break, the Chamber will start and you'll have to wait until the next break. The Chamber considers this to be a waiver of your right to be present in court. So next time we'll not wait as we did today nine minutes. We'll just start. You can follow the proceedings, if you wish, from a cell with a screen and you would then of course be welcome again after the next break. This having said, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Mladic apparently wants to consult with counsel which he can during the next break or write a small note to counsel and then it will be passed on to counsel. Mr. Groome, there was an issue about scheduling next week. The Chamber -- the Judges have looked in their agendas and the best opportunities to gain some extra time would be on Monday and Tuesday. The Chamber would like you to come up with a concrete plan, that is, because just adding an hour to a morning session is not possible, as you may aware of due to staff supporting us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore could you prepare a plan and perhaps discuss it already with Mr. Lukic so that we can use some extra time, but preferably focus on Monday and Tuesday afternoons for the extra time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Lukic, if you're ready please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sivac, I am going to ask you about Ljubija next. Is it correct that the Muslims replaced by force the Croat who was at the helm of the police station in Ljubija in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have in mind Branko Bjekic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, according to the information I have, in Ljubija at the time a staff of sorts was established, not a Crisis Staff, but this one comprised Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. They decided to have Branko Bjekic removed because he was commander in the previous communist regime. Amongst themselves, they had agreed to have Fikret Sarajlic take over that position who had been an active-duty policeman in Prijedor. After the take-over by Serbs in Prijedor he was kicked out as well. He hails from Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 8, please, of the document before us, 1D411. It is transcript page 6782. I'm interested in lines 23 through 25 at the bottom of the page and then we'll move on to the next lines 1 through 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this testimony you say: "In Ljubija in May 1992, Branko Bjekic was removed. He was a police commander in Ljubija, a Croat by nationality. He was replaced by Fikret Sarajlic who had been dismissed from his job in Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I read "exchanged" instead of "removed."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then I will read in English. Maybe I didn't translate properly. "In Ljubija in May 1992, Branko Bjekic was exchanged. He was a police commander in Ljubija, a Croat by nationality. He was replaced by Fikret Sarajlic who had been dismissed from his job in Prijedor and he was assisted by Drago Tokmadzic, Ismet Taric, Aziz Aliskovic, and Velid Krupic. In this way, they took over the police station in Ljubija. Is that correct?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer: [In English] "Yes, for a very short time. They did not agree to be commanded by Simo Drljaca, and the extremists from the Serbian Democratic Party who had taken over the police station in Prijedor." [Interpretation] All of the persons you mentioned here, save for Drago Tokmadzic, were Muslim; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Drago Tokmadzic was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just now you told us that a staff was established comprising all ethnicities, that is to say Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. Can you tell us who was there on behalf of the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I forgot to mention at the time the name of Curguz. I know him under the nickname of Krivi. He was a Serb. There was a Komosar person, another Serb, from the police station. I have to tell you, though, that this sort of staff was active in Ljubija for only a few days. In only several days that police station was put under sub-control from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today that Curguz, aka Krivi, and the Komosar person - and you say they were both Serbs - participated in the removal of Branko Bjekic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who participated in his removal by name. I do know that he was removed. I only mentioned the policemen I knew well with whom I used to work in the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was to leave this topic briefly. You were asked whether your cousin Adnan took some packages to Slavko Ecimovic, be it in person or with the assistance of Dr. Esad or Hamed Cuk. Is that piece of information correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Slavko Ecimovic headed the attack or, as you call it, an attempt of liberating Prijedor; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any participation in providing assistance to the fighters headed by Ecimovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none whatsoever. I even had a difference of views with Slavko Ecimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the leadership of the SDA and of the SDS in Prijedor had agreed on the take-over and that Mirza Mujadzic, SDA president, took part in those talks?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDA and the SDS, whether they had any arrangements in place?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, about the take-over of power so as to have it done without fighting.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received that information from a third source and perhaps I mentioned it in one of my previous statements. I stand by it in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mirza Mujadzic had sent his family out of Prijedor before the conflict erupted; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but so did many other people from Prijedor, other Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
